metadata.note: The Milwaukee Road's Chicago - Twin Cities - Aberdeen main line: the eastern 700 miles of the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific's transcontinental route, the line the Olympian and Olympian Hiawatha ran on their way to Seattle and Tacoma. Chicago-Milwaukee-La Crosse-Winona-St. Paul is the same physical railroad as the Twin Cities Hiawatha in milwaukee_road_hiawatha.geojson, and that file's geometry (Amtrak GTFS-sourced for the corridor) is reused here for the eastern half. West of St. Paul the geometry is the real ex-Milwaukee track centerline, routed over OpenStreetMap rail data through Minneapolis, Hopkins, Cologne, Norwood Young America, Glencoe, Olivia, Granite Falls, Montevideo, Appleton (TC&W Glencoe Subdivision), then Ortonville, Milbank, Summit, Waubay, Webster, Bristol, Andover and Groton to Aberdeen (BNSF Appleton Subdivision) - the line built by the Hastings & Dakota Railway and pushed into Dakota Territory by the Milwaukee Road, most of which is still in service. Era boundaries follow real, sourced milestones (line construction, the Pacific Extension, named-train introductions and discontinuations); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not real timetables.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympian_Hiawatha (route via Milwaukee, Portage, Wisconsin Dells, Tomah, La Crosse, Winona, St. Paul, Minneapolis, Montevideo, Aberdeen, Mobridge; the Olympian ran May 28 1911-1947, the Olympian Hiawatha June 29 1947-May 22 1961; trains 15/16 continued unnamed Minneapolis-Deer Lodge, cut back to a coach-only train to Aberdeen in 1964 and discontinued April 17 1969)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen_station_(Milwaukee_Road) (1911 brick depot replaced an earlier wooden one, built as a division point with railroad offices upstairs; last passenger train for Minneapolis April 17 1969; largest railway station in South Dakota)

https://aberdeenmag.com/2021/10/happy-birthday-aberdeen-established-1881-1880-1882-1883/ (Aberdeen plat notarized Oct 30 1880 and registered Jan 3 1881; graded to Aberdeen on the James River by Dec 1880; first Milwaukee Road train arrived July 6 1881, the date the Dacotah Prairie Museum uses as the town's birthday)
https://www.american-rails.com/pce.html (Pacific Coast Extension built from Mobridge SD, completed May 14 1909, 1,440 miles Mobridge-Tacoma)

https://www.american-rails.com/sd.html and http://genealogytrails.com/sdak/railroads.html (Hastings & Dakota Railway built west from Hastings, reaching Glencoe by 1872 and later Ortonville; sold to the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul in January 1880, which then built west across Dakota Territory through Milbank, Bristol and Andover)
OpenStreetMap (track centerline west of St. Paul, via the TC&W Glencoe Subdivision and BNSF Appleton Subdivision, ODbL)

segments.note: Two separate railroads at this point. In the east the Milwaukee & St. Paul completed its own Chicago-Milwaukee line in 1873, giving it a through Chicago-Twin Cities route (see milwaukee_road_hiawatha.geojson). In the west the Hastings & Dakota Railway, chartered 1867, was building out of Hastings across southern Minnesota, reaching Glencoe by 1872 and eventually pushing on toward Ortonville on the Dakota line. (Full Chicago-Aberdeen route shown regardless of the year each section opened.) estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul bought the Hastings & Dakota in January 1880 and drove it west out of Ortonville into Dakota Territory through Milbank and Bristol, platting a town every five to ten miles as it went. By December 1880 the grade had reached Aberdeen on the James River. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The first Milwaukee Road train rolled into Aberdeen July 6 1881 - the date the town still counts as its birthday - after the plat was registered that January. Aberdeen grew into the railroad's Dakota hub and a division point, and the line west from the Twin Cities became the road's main artery onto the northern plains. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Pacific Coast Extension was completed May 14 1909, running 1,440 miles from Mobridge, South Dakota to Tacoma. Overnight this Chicago-Aberdeen line stopped being a prairie trunk route and became the eastern leg of a Chicago-Puget Sound transcontinental railroad. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Olympian entered service May 28 1911, Chicago to Seattle and Tacoma via Milwaukee, La Crosse, the Twin Cities, Montevideo, Aberdeen and Mobridge. Aberdeen got a new brick depot the same year, replacing a wooden one and housing division offices upstairs; it is still the largest railway station in South Dakota. The company was renamed Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific in 1928. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The streamlined Olympian Hiawatha replaced the Olympian June 29 1947, running full-length Chicago-Seattle with Skytop lounge observation cars, and was the Milwaukee Road's transcontinental flagship until it was discontinued May 22 1961. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Cut back in 1964 to a coach-only train running no farther west than Aberdeen. The last passenger train left Aberdeen for Minneapolis April 17 1969, two years before Amtrak, which never took the route. The tracks remain: TC&W runs the Minneapolis-Appleton half and BNSF the Appleton-Aberdeen half, where Aberdeen still hosts the largest yard in South Dakota. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
